modules.title: Advanced Indexing
modules.goal: Use specialized indexes and index-only access without over-indexing the database.

topics.title: Index Types Review
topics.simple: B-tree, hash, GIN, GiST aur BRIN alag workloads ke liye hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL index types target different data shapes: B-tree for ordered scalars, hash for equality, GIN for composites, GiST for ranges and BRIN for correlated large tables.
points: Match the type to the data.

example.sql: SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'students';

topics.title: B-tree Deep Dive
topics.simple: B-tree ordered comparisons aur ranges support karta hai.
topics.pro: A B-tree keeps keys ordered, supporting equality, ranges, prefix LIKE and ORDER BY.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks ON students (marks DESC);

topics.title: Composite Index Order
topics.simple: Composite index ka order left-to-right use hota hai.
topics.pro: A composite B-tree can serve queries on its leading columns; later columns are useful only when earlier ones are constrained.
points: A skipped leading column weakens use.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_student_course ON enrollments (student_id, course_id);

topics.title: Covering Indexes
topics.simple: INCLUDE payload columns index-only scan dete hain.
topics.pro: INCLUDE adds non-key columns so the index can satisfy a query without heap access.
points: INCLUDE is not part of the key.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_include ON students (marks) INCLUDE (name);

topics.title: Partial Indexes
topics.simple: Partial index predicate se index chhota hota hai.
topics.pro: A partial index stores only rows matching its WHERE clause and is useful for rare or active subsets.
points: The query must imply the predicate.
It speeds writes versus a full index.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_high_marks ON students (marks) WHERE marks >= 90;

topics.title: Expression Indexes
topics.simple: Expression index computed values ko index karta hai.
topics.pro: An expression index stores a function result, such as LOWER(email), and serves queries using the same expression.
points: It is useful for case-insensitive lookups.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_lower_email ON students (LOWER(email));

topics.title: GIN Indexes
topics.simple: GIN composite values ke containment ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GIN builds an inverted index for arrays, JSONB and text search, accelerating containment and existence operators.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_name_gin ON students USING gin (to_tsvector('simple', name));

topics.title: GiST Indexes
topics.simple: GiST ranges, geometry aur nearest-neighbor ke liye hai.
topics.pro: GiST supports balanced search trees over complex types and powers exclusion constraints.

example.sql:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date_gist ON enrollments USING gist (enrolled_on);

topics.title: BRIN Indexes
topics.simple: BRIN large ordered tables ke liye compact hai.
topics.pro: BRIN stores block-range summaries, making it tiny and effective when a column correlates with physical order, such as timestamps.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_enrollments_date_brin ON enrollments USING brin (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Hash Indexes
topics.simple: Hash index equality-only lookup deta hai.
topics.pro: A hash index stores hash codes and supports equality, but not ordering or ranges.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_email_hash ON students USING hash (email);

topics.title: Index-Only Scans
topics.simple: Index-only scan heap visit bachata hai.
topics.pro: When all requested columns are in the index and the visibility map is favorable, PostgreSQL can answer from the index alone.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
example.output: An Index Only Scan when covered.

topics.title: Index Bloat
topics.simple: Updates index bloat create karte hain.
topics.pro: Dead index entries accumulate after updates and deletes, increasing size and slowing scans until cleanup.

example.sql: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_students_marks'));

topics.title: REINDEX
topics.simple: REINDEX index rebuild karta hai.
topics.pro: REINDEX rebuilds an index to remove bloat or repair corruption; it can lock the index or table.

example.sql: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_marks;

topics.title: Concurrent Index Creation
topics.simple: CONCURRENTLY live writes allow karta hai.
topics.pro: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes but takes longer and cannot run in a transaction block.
points: Can fail and leave an invalid index.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_students_marks ON students (marks);

topics.title: Index Selectivity
topics.simple: Selectivity index ki usefulness batati hai.
topics.pro: An index is most useful when the predicate returns a small fraction of rows; low selectivity may favor a sequential scan.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT marks)::numeric / COUNT(*) FROM students;

topics.title: Multi-Column Selectivity
topics.simple: Combined predicates index order decide karte hain.
topics.pro: The planner estimates combined selectivity, so index columns should match the most common equality and range combinations.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_name ON students (marks, name);

topics.title: Common Advanced Mistakes
topics.simple: Over-indexing, wrong opclass aur unused indexes common mistakes hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are adding indexes for every column, using GIN where B-tree fits, and never checking index usage.

example.sql: SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan;

topics.title: Monitoring Indexes
topics.simple: pg_stat_user_indexes usage dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Index statistics show scans and tuple reads, helping identify unused or ineffective indexes.

example.sql: SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes;

topics.title: Practical Tuning
topics.simple: Slow query se index plan tak.
topics.pro: A disciplined tuning loop captures the query, reads its plan, adds the smallest useful index and measures again.

example.sql: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90 ORDER BY marks DESC;
example.output: A plan with timing and buffer use.

topics.title: Index Maintenance Plan
topics.simple: Indexes ko create, monitor aur retire karo.
topics.pro: A production index plan includes creation standards, usage review, bloat monitoring and safe removal of unused indexes.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Types Review in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL index types target different data shapes: B-tree for ordered scalars, hash for equality, GIN for composites, GiST for ranges and BRIN for correlated large tables. Key rules: Match the type to the data. B-tree is the default. Specialized indexes need operator classes.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain B-tree Deep Dive in a production query.
interview.answer: A B-tree keeps keys ordered, supporting equality, ranges, prefix LIKE and ORDER BY. Key rules: It is balanced. It supports ordering. It handles duplicates.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Composite Index Order in a production query.
interview.answer: A composite B-tree can serve queries on its leading columns; later columns are useful only when earlier ones are constrained. Key rules: Put equality first. Ranges come later. A skipped leading column weakens use.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Covering Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: INCLUDE adds non-key columns so the index can satisfy a query without heap access. Key rules: INCLUDE is not part of the key. It increases size. Visibility map affects index-only scans.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Partial Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: A partial index stores only rows matching its WHERE clause and is useful for rare or active subsets. Key rules: The query must imply the predicate. It saves space. It speeds writes versus a full index.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Expression Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: An expression index stores a function result, such as LOWER(email), and serves queries using the same expression. Key rules: Match the expression. It is useful for case-insensitive lookups. It costs write CPU.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain GIN Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: GIN builds an inverted index for arrays, JSONB and text search, accelerating containment and existence operators. Key rules: Good for @>, ?, @@. Updates can be expensive. Choose the right opclass.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain GiST Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: GiST supports balanced search trees over complex types and powers exclusion constraints. Key rules: Good for ranges. Supports KNN. Needs the right extension.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain BRIN Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: BRIN stores block-range summaries, making it tiny and effective when a column correlates with physical order, such as timestamps. Key rules: Very small. Good for append-only data. Less precise than B-tree.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Hash Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: A hash index stores hash codes and supports equality, but not ordering or ranges. Key rules: Equality only. Rarely better than B-tree. It cannot support ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index-Only Scans in a production query.
interview.answer: When all requested columns are in the index and the visibility map is favorable, PostgreSQL can answer from the index alone. Key rules: Use INCLUDE. VACUUM maintains visibility. Check EXPLAIN for Heap Fetches.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Bloat in a production query.
interview.answer: Dead index entries accumulate after updates and deletes, increasing size and slowing scans until cleanup. Key rules: Monitor size. VACUUM regularly. REINDEX when needed.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain REINDEX in a production query.
interview.answer: REINDEX rebuilds an index to remove bloat or repair corruption; it can lock the index or table. Key rules: Use CONCURRENTLY when available. It needs free space. It can be slow.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Concurrent Index Creation in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes but takes longer and cannot run in a transaction block. Key rules: Avoids write locks. Can fail and leave an invalid index. Run outside a transaction.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: An index is most useful when the predicate returns a small fraction of rows; low selectivity may favor a sequential scan. Key rules: High selectivity is better. Statistics matter. Test with real data.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Multi-Column Selectivity in a production query.
interview.answer: The planner estimates combined selectivity, so index columns should match the most common equality and range combinations. Key rules: Equality columns first. Range columns later. Read the plan.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Common Advanced Mistakes in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are adding indexes for every column, using GIN where B-tree fits, and never checking index usage. Key rules: Measure usage. Match operator classes. Drop unused indexes.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Monitoring Indexes in a production query.
interview.answer: Index statistics show scans and tuple reads, helping identify unused or ineffective indexes. Key rules: Check idx_scan. Reset stats after changes. Correlate with query load.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Practical Tuning in a production query.
interview.answer: A disciplined tuning loop captures the query, reads its plan, adds the smallest useful index and measures again. Key rules: Capture the query. Read the plan. Add one index. Measure before and after.

interview.q: Module 26 · Explain Index Maintenance Plan in a production query.
interview.answer: A production index plan includes creation standards, usage review, bloat monitoring and safe removal of unused indexes. Key rules: Name consistently. Build concurrently. Review usage monthly. Drop with evidence.

logic.q: Module 26 · Why does Index Bloat matter?
logic.answer: Dead index entries accumulate after updates and deletes, increasing size and slowing scans until cleanup. Monitor size. VACUUM regularly. REINDEX when needed.
REINDEX rebuilds an index to remove bloat or repair corruption; it can lock the index or table. Use CONCURRENTLY when available. It needs free space. It can be slow.

logic.q: Module 26 · Why does Concurrent Index Creation matter?
logic.answer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes but takes longer and cannot run in a transaction block. Avoids write locks. Can fail and leave an invalid index. Run outside a transaction.

logic.q: Module 26 · Why does Index Selectivity matter?
logic.answer: An index is most useful when the predicate returns a small fraction of rows; low selectivity may favor a sequential scan. High selectivity is better. Statistics matter. Test with real data.

debug.title: Wrong operator class
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX idx_title ON courses USING gin (title);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_title_fts ON courses USING gin (to_tsvector('english', title));
debug.error: data type text has no default operator class for access method "gin"

debug.title: BRIN on random data
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX idx_students_marks_brin ON students USING brin (marks);
debug.error: BRIN is ineffective when values are not physically correlated

debug.title: Covering index wrong column
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_students_name ON students (marks) INCLUDE (email);
SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_students_name ON students (marks) INCLUDE (name);
debug.error: The requested column is not covered

debug.title: Partial predicate mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_high ON students (marks) WHERE marks > 90;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_high ON students (marks) WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.error: The query predicate does not imply the partial predicate

debug.title: Expression mismatch
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_lower ON students (LOWER(name));
SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM students WHERE LOWER(name) = LOWER('Aarav');
debug.error: The expression index is not used by the plain predicate

debug.title: Invalid concurrent index
debug.broken: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_bad ON students (missing_column);
debug.fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_bad ON students (marks);

debug.title: Reindex in transaction
debug.error: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block

debug.title: Unused index
debug.fix: Review the index and drop it only after confirming no query depends on it.
debug.error: The index still consumes writes and space

debug.title: Hash range query
debug.broken:
CREATE INDEX idx_marks_hash ON students USING hash (marks);
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 90;
debug.error: The hash index cannot serve a range predicate

debug.title: Too many indexes
debug.fix: Keep only indexes used by real queries and verify with pg_stat_user_indexes.
